body:
What is prehistoric art?

Prehistory refers to the period before written records became available for reconstructing human life in a particular region. Archaeologists study this period through stone tools, bones, habitation remains, pottery and artistic expressions preserved on natural surfaces.

Prehistoric art includes paintings, drawings and engravings made by early human communities. In India, rock paintings are particularly important because they preserve evidence of how people observed animals, represented activities and communicated visually.

The earliest reported rock paintings in India are associated with the Upper Palaeolithic period. Artistic activity continued through the Mesolithic, Chalcolithic and later historical periods. A rock shelter may therefore contain paintings created by different communities over a very long time.

Distinguishing the principal forms

Rock painting: An image produced by applying pigment to a natural rock surface.

Rock engraving: An image produced by cutting, scratching or incising lines into rock.

Relief sculpture: A carved figure that projects from a background surface while remaining attached to it.

Free-standing sculpture: A three-dimensional object that can generally be viewed from multiple directions.

These distinctions are important because an image painted on the wall of a natural shelter is not the same as a figure carved into the wall of a temple. Both are visual arts, but their materials, methods and historical contexts differ.

Chronological background

Palaeolithic period

The Palaeolithic, or Old Stone Age, is associated with hunting, gathering and the production of stone tools. The Upper Palaeolithic phase provides some of the earliest evidence of rock painting in India. Animals were important subjects, often represented through outlines and simplified forms.

Mesolithic period

The Mesolithic period is associated with small stone tools called microliths. Rock paintings from this phase frequently show hunters carrying bows and arrows, people working together, community dances and activities involving animals.

Chalcolithic period

The Chalcolithic, or Copper-Stone Age, includes communities that used copper alongside stone tools. At some rock-art sites, paintings suggest contact with settled farming populations. Pottery designs, geometric patterns and representations of objects associated with settled life become relevant.

These archaeological periods do not begin and end on identical dates everywhere in India. Their identification depends on regional evidence. A painting cannot be assigned a secure date simply because it depicts hunting or farming.

How prehistoric art helps reconstruct society

Paintings of animals provide clues about the environment familiar to their makers. Hunting scenes suggest methods of obtaining food and possible cooperation among individuals. Representations of dancing, gathering food and family-like groups indicate that prehistoric artistic subjects extended beyond hunting.

Nevertheless, a picture is not a complete record of society. For example, the presence of hunting scenes does not establish that every inhabitant was a hunter or that the entire community followed one fixed way of life.

Evidence and interpretation

Archaeologists compare paintings with tools, habitation deposits and other remains from the surrounding area. They also examine the position of images on the rock, differences in pigments and the superimposition of one painting over another.

Superimposition occurs when a newer image is painted over an older one. It can help establish which image was made earlier at that particular location. However, it does not automatically provide an absolute date in years.

Some prehistoric paintings may have recorded daily experiences, while others may have carried ceremonial or symbolic meanings. Their exact purposes are not always recoverable from archaeological evidence.

Prelims focus

  • The earliest reported Indian rock paintings belong to the Upper Palaeolithic tradition.
  • Mesolithic paintings commonly depict hunting, animals and group activities.
  • Chalcolithic rock art may show contact with farming communities.
  • Rock painting uses pigment; rock engraving involves cutting or scratching a surface.
  • Trap: A prehistoric natural rock shelter is not the same as a later rock-cut temple or monastery.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class XI, Chapter 1, 'Prehistoric Rock Paintings', printed pp. 1–7; NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class VI, Chapter 2, 'On the Trail of the Earliest People'.]

title: Prehistoric Art: Meaning, Forms and Historical Evidence

body:
Location and importance

Bhimbetka is situated in the Vindhyan Hills of Madhya Pradesh, approximately 45 km south of Bhopal. Its sandstone formations contain natural rock shelters used and decorated by human communities over different periods.

Archaeologist V. S. Wakankar brought the shelters to archaeological attention through his investigations beginning in 1957–58. Subsequent research established Bhimbetka as one of India's most important prehistoric rock-art complexes.

Bhimbetka is significant because paintings, occupation evidence and the surrounding landscape can be examined together. The shelters are not isolated paintings removed from their original setting.

Phases of rock painting

The paintings at Bhimbetka represent different periods. A commonly taught classification identifies an Upper Palaeolithic phase, a Mesolithic phase and a Chalcolithic phase, followed by later historical paintings.

PhasePrincipal featuresTypical subjects
Upper PalaeolithicLarge figures, comparatively simple outlines and linear representationsLarge wild animals and simplified human figures
MesolithicSmaller figures, greater variety and detailed group activityHunting, dancing, animals, honey collection and community life
ChalcolithicGreater connection with settled agricultural communitiesGeometric motifs, pottery-related patterns and objects associated with settled life
Later historical phasesAdditional paintings made after the prehistoric phasesLater social and ceremonial subjects

Subjects depicted in the paintings

Animals

Paintings include bison, deer, wild boar, elephants, tigers, rhinoceroses and other animals. Some are shown individually, while others appear as part of hunting or movement scenes.

Animal figures are often more carefully modelled than human figures. Their size and proportions sometimes differ from those of nearby human figures. This difference may reflect artistic emphasis rather than the actual relative size of the subjects.

Hunting scenes

Mesolithic paintings frequently show hunters carrying bows, arrows, spears and pointed sticks. Some figures appear to use traps or snares. Group hunting scenes indicate that artists could represent coordinated activity rather than only individual subjects.

Social activities

Other scenes represent people dancing, gathering honey or fruit, preparing food and participating in activities involving adults and children. Handprints, fingertip marks and geometric designs also occur.

The variety of subjects shows that rock art should not be understood merely as a record of hunting. It also preserves visual expressions of community life.

UNESCO World Heritage status

The Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2003 under cultural criteria (iii) and (v). The inscribed property contains 5 clusters of natural rock shelters.

UNESCO identifies the relationship between people and the landscape, as well as the evidence of hunting-and-gathering traditions, as central to the site's significance. Its description specifically highlights paintings dating from the Mesolithic period through historical times.

The UNESCO inscription concerns the archaeological and cultural landscape; it does not mean that every painting in the complex belongs to a single period.

Prelims focus

  • Bhimbetka is in Madhya Pradesh, in the Vindhyan Hills south of Bhopal.
  • V. S. Wakankar investigated the shelters from 1957–58.
  • Mesolithic paintings prominently feature small human figures, hunting and group activities.
  • Bhimbetka was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2003.
  • The UNESCO property includes 5 clusters of natural rock shelters.
  • Trap: Bhimbetka is in Madhya Pradesh, not Gujarat.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class XI, Chapter 1, printed pp. 3–7; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka', World Heritage List no. 925, inscription 2003, consulted 23 November 2026; Ministry of Culture, Government of India, 'Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka', consulted 23 November 2026.]

body:
How prehistoric pigments were prepared

Prehistoric painters used naturally available minerals to produce colours. They ground suitable rocks or minerals into powder and then prepared a mixture that could be applied to stone.

Red ochre was commonly obtained from iron-rich minerals, particularly haematite, traditionally called geru. Green pigment could be derived from a green variety of chalcedony. White pigment may have been prepared from limestone or similar materials.

The powder may have been combined with water and binding substances such as gum, resin or animal fat. Plant fibres could be used to apply the colours. These possibilities are reconstructed from archaeological and material evidence; the precise preparation method of every surviving painting is not known.

Red and white were especially common at Bhimbetka, although other colours also occur. Paintings have survived because suitable mineral pigments, rock surfaces and environmental conditions sometimes preserve them for long periods.

Lakhudiyar: A major site in Uttarakhand

Lakhudiyar is a prehistoric rock-art site near Almora in Uttarakhand, associated with rock shelters along the Suyal River. Its paintings differ from Bhimbetka in their individual arrangements and motifs.

The paintings at Lakhudiyar include stick-like human figures, animals, geometric forms, groups of dots and wavy lines. A particularly recognisable subject is a group of human figures holding hands in a dancing formation.

Black, red ochre and white paintings are present. At some locations, superimposition establishes a sequence in which black paintings precede red ones, which are in turn covered by white paintings.

The black-red-white sequence is an observation about particular paintings at Lakhudiyar. It must not be treated as a universal chronological rule for all Indian rock-art sites.

Other regions with prehistoric rock paintings

Prehistoric paintings and engravings have been reported from several parts of the Indian subcontinent. Important concentrations occur in the Vindhyan ranges of Madhya Pradesh and their Kaimur extensions into Uttar Pradesh.

Other sites have been reported in Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar and the Kumaon region of Uttarakhand. Suitable rock surfaces, available pigments and prehistoric human activity together help explain why particular landscapes preserve rock art.

What superimposition tells us

At some rock-art sites, newer images cover earlier ones. Bhimbetka contains examples of multiple layers, and some locations have been described as having as many as 20 superimposed layers.

Superimposition can establish relative chronology: the image underneath was generally created before the image covering it. Determining an absolute date may require additional archaeological evidence and scientific methods.

Interpreting themes without overstating conclusions

Rock paintings can suggest knowledge of local fauna, group activities and changing ways of life. For example, representations of hunting equipment may help identify methods of obtaining food, while geometric designs similar to pottery motifs may suggest cultural interaction.

However, it is usually difficult to decide whether a scene is an everyday record, a symbolic expression or part of a ritual. A dancing scene does not establish the exact occasion of the dance. Likewise, a painted animal cannot automatically be identified as a sacred animal.

The strongest historical interpretation combines the painting with the archaeological context in which it survives.

Prelims focus

  • Haematite is associated with red ochre pigment.
  • Plant fibres could be used for applying prehistoric colours.
  • Lakhudiyar is near Almora in Uttarakhand, along the Suyal River.
  • Linked dancing human figures are an important Lakhudiyar motif.
  • Superimposition helps establish relative sequence, not necessarily absolute dates.
  • Trap: The colour of a painting alone does not securely determine its age.

[Source: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class XI, Chapter 1, 'Prehistoric Rock Paintings', printed pp. 2–7.]
